html:
In 1696 the Dutch East India Company brought coffee seedlings from Malabar in India to Java. After a flood killed the first plants, a second shipment in 1699 took root, and within a few decades Java was a major supplier of coffee to Europe.

Until then nearly all coffee came from Yemen through the port of Mocha; see Coffee drinking in Yemen and the Mocha monsoon fair. The Dutch wanted their own supply. Coffee had reached Malabar earlier, smuggled from Yemen; see Coffee in Chikmagalur.

At first Javanese rulers were made to deliver set amounts. In the 1800s the Cultivation System forced villagers to grow coffee and other export crops for the colonial state, causing hardship and famine. The novel Max Havelaar of 1860 attacked this system. Java's coffee was hit by leaf rust in the late 1800s, the disease that also ruined Ceylon's; see Coffee rust in Ceylon. The name "java" for coffee still recalls the island. Coffee was also carried from Dutch gardens to the Americas; see Coffee comes to Brazil.
